content.content: The Republic Falls

Elections still happen, in form. Courts still sit, in form. But the guardrails are gone. The rules no longer bind the people who write them, and the opposition, ours and everyone's, operates at their sufferance.
It did not happen in a day. It happened in a thousand small accommodations, ignored warnings, and failures of nerve, by us and by others.
We conserve our energy and watch the news cycle go by.
Defending the Republic
The Democrats, 2014-2026
Social Democracy: An Alternate History

You are the strategists, donors, organizers, and elected leaders of the Democratic Party. The Obama coalition looks unbeatable on paper. It is not. Over the next twelve years you will face a populist insurgency on the right, a restless insurgency on the left, a pandemic, an attempted overturning of an election, and the slow grind of institutions under stress.
Your primary goal is to keep American democracy standing. Winning elections is how you do it, but it is not the same thing.

With a Democrat in the White House, the 2020 nomination is a formality. The question is whether the coalition will hold together through a pandemic and a divided country.
We name specific causes and propose specific fixes.
New faces, new ideas, and a new set of disagreements.

A Second Term
The incumbent has won re-election. The movement is emboldened. The opposition must find a way to resist for four more years.
The package passes without a single Republican vote. The economy roars back. So, eventually, do prices.
We hold. The shutdown drags on, and the pressure builds on both sides.
Nobody is pleased, but everyone is in the room.

content.content: Repeal and Replace
The Republican majorities attempt to repeal the Affordable Care Act. In the Senate the margin is a single vote. Town halls fill with angry constituents. Our base is watching.
Engineers are brought in. By spring the site works, and enrollment surges. The story shifts, slowly.
The after-action review is long. The damage is done.

afghanistan.title: Kabul
afghanistan.subtitle: The longest war ends in chaos.

content.content: Kabul

The withdrawal from Afghanistan collapses into a frantic evacuation. A suicide bombing kills thirteen service members. The pictures are devastating. The policy had wide public support. The execution did not.
The president withdraws. The Vice President is the nominee. The energy returns. So does the time pressure.

capitol_attack.prosecute.subtitle: Courts and the rule of law.

content.content: Hundreds of rioters are prosecuted.
Counter-protests grow. Some are peaceful. Some are not. The fringes feed on each other.
We follow public-health guidance. A noisy minority resists.
The standoff stretches to the last minute.
The Debt Ceiling
The new House majority demands cuts in exchange for raising the debt ceiling. The Treasury warns of default. The Constitution says the debt must be paid.
We offer bipartisan ground.

dem_inaug_2017.title: A Democratic Inauguration
dem_inaug_2017.subtitle: Alt-history: we hold the White House.

content.content: A Democratic Inauguration

A Democratic president takes the oath. The coalition held, narrowly. The Republican Party's internal fight over its populist wing is only beginning. The question now is whether we can govern, and whether we can keep the opposition inside the rules.
We say, accurately, that a foreign government is trying to influence our election. Some hear it as an excuse.
Referendums in several states show the issue is more popular than many expected.

options.title: Take the fight to state ballot measures.

content.content: Dobbs
The Supreme Court overturns Roe v. Wade. Abortion is now a state-by-state fight. For the first time in a generation, many Democratic voters feel an urgent reason to turn out.
States pass laws limiting cooperation. The federal-state conflict deepens.

options.title: Pass state laws to limit cooperation.

content.content: Enforcement

A surge of federal immigration enforcement in major cities provokes protests, standoffs with local police, and fatal shootings. The administration says it is restoring order. The opposition says it is breaking the law. A divided public watches.
We condemn violence, defend the right to protest, and call for federal review. Everybody is a little unsatisfied.
The slogan is more popular on social media than it is at the ballot box.
The administration is pressured. Some donors are furious.
We argue that restraint now will help prices later.
The campaign committee backs the candidates best suited to their districts. The party is, for once, more flexible than its reputation.
We argue for process and accept the result.

kavanaugh.title: The Confirmation
kavanaugh.subtitle: A Supreme Court fight and an allegation.

options.title: Press for a thorough investigation, then stand down.

content.content: The Confirmation

A Supreme Court nominee faces credible allegations of sexual misconduct from his youth. The Senate hearing becomes a national drama. The nominee is confirmed on a narrow vote. The midterms are weeks away.
We invest in persuasion and message testing.
We say what many are thinking. We do not win the votes.

obergefell.subtitle: Marriage equality and a massacre in Charleston.

options.title: Speak to the moment, not the factions.

content.content: A Landmark Summer
In one week, a gunman murders nine people at a church in Charleston and the Supreme Court rules that same-sex couples have a constitutional right to marry. Grief and celebration share a news cycle.
Funds flow to local security.
The race is long and the nominee is bruised, but the party is energized and the left feels respected. She still wins, narrowly.
The nomination goes to the former vice president. The campaign was long but the left felt heard.
The Vice President takes the nomination.
The Nominee
The incumbent Republican administration is deeply unpopular in some quarters and beloved in others. The party must choose a standard-bearer for 2024.
A smaller package passes with a few bipartisan votes. The recovery is slower.

rescue_plan.title: The Rescue Plan
rescue_plan.subtitle: Relief, reconciliation, and the debate over size.

content.content: The Rescue Plan
With a narrow trifecta, we can pass a large pandemic-relief package through budget reconciliation. Moderates worry about the size. Progressives want more.
A deal is struck, with a promise to vote on the subsidies later. The base is not pleased.

shutdown_2025.title: Shutdown
shutdown_2025.subtitle: A standoff over health care subsidies.

content.content: Shutdown

The government shuts down for weeks in a fight over expiring health-insurance subsidies. Federal workers go unpaid. Flights are delayed. Both sides claim the moral high ground. In November, elections in New Jersey and Virginia go strongly to our side, and a democratic socialist wins the New York City mayoralty.
The leadership prevails. The left grumbles.
We argue that the government is not following the law. Many voters agree and many do not care.
Researchers and rapid-response staff are hired early. The files are thick by the fall.

Courts matter, and so do the people who staff the government.

November 2026. The country is divided, tired, and often furious. But the institutions have held. Courts rule, officials certify, and power changes hands when voters say so. The coalition has learned some hard lessons about governing and about losing.
Congress is in our hands.
We hold the House.
We hold the Senate.
We are in the minority in both chambers, but the republic is intact.

options.title: Defend the law and the substance.
Fix it quietly and let results speak.

content.content: The Rollout

The Affordable Care Act's central promise is that the uninsured can finally buy coverage. In practice, the website has struggled and millions of people have had their plans cancelled. Our opponents are gleeful. Our own side is worried.
An open process might have produced a better candidate. It might have produced chaos.

options.title: Withdraw and call for an open convention.

content.content: The Debate

A June debate goes badly. For weeks, an elderly president's stamina has been quietly questioned. Now it is on every screen. Donors, members of Congress, and ordinary voters are asking whether he should continue.
We say we will focus on the economy. The wound does not close.

options.title: Move on and focus on governing.

content.content: January 6th

A mob, stirred by false claims that the election was stolen, breaks into the Capitol while Congress is certifying the results. Lawmakers shelter in place. Police are beaten. Hours later, Congress finishes the job. Many Republican members still vote to object to the results.
Civil libertarians worry about the tools. Law enforcement welcomes the attention.

charlottesville.title: Charlottesville
charlottesville.subtitle: A rally, a killing, a president's response.

options.title: Confront the far right in the streets.

content.content: Charlottesville

Torch-bearing white supremacists march through a Virginia college town. One of them drives a car into a crowd of counter-protesters, killing a woman. The president's response draws bipartisan criticism. Organized extremism has stepped out of the shadows.
We expand access to the ballot. Opponents allege fraud, without evidence.

covid.title: The Pandemic
covid.subtitle: A new coronavirus spreads across the world.

options.title: Fight for mail-in voting and expanded early voting.

content.content: The Pandemic
A new coronavirus is spreading. By March, schools and offices close. Hospitals are overwhelmed. Everything about politics changes: campaigns, conventions, voting itself.
The party hires real security professionals. Too late for this cycle, in time for the next.

options.title: Apologize, replace the chair, and move on.

content.content: The Leak

Thousands of internal party e-mails appear on a transparency website. U.S. intelligence agencies will later attribute the hack to Russian military intelligence. The e-mails show staffers disparaging the insurgent campaign. The convention opens in disarray.

ferguson.quiet.subtitle: Avoids a fight, loses some trust.

content.content: Silence is read as indifference by some and prudence by others.

ferguson.title: Ferguson
ferguson.subtitle: A shooting, a grand jury, and a movement.

options.title: Back the protesters and the call for reform.
Call for calm and reform together.
Stay quiet. Let the DOJ do its work.

content.content: Ferguson

The killing of Michael Brown by a police officer in Ferguson, Missouri, sets off protests that spread across the country. The questions are about policing, race, and accountability. The party has to decide how to speak.
We say reform, not abolition. Activists are unsatisfied.
A Summer of Protest

A police officer kneels on George Floyd's neck for nine minutes. The video spreads worldwide. Protests fill cities for weeks. Most are peaceful. Some end in looting and burning. A slogan about defunding the police dominates the debate.
Youth turnout is a concern.

gaza_split.title: A Divided Party
gaza_split.subtitle: War in the Middle East splits the coalition.

content.content: A Divided Party

After the October 7th attacks on Israel and the war in Gaza that follows, the Democratic coalition splits. Young voters and progressives press for a ceasefire. Older voters and many in leadership support Israel. Campuses erupt. Antisemitism and Islamophobia both rise.
"Transitory" will be remembered.

options.title: Focus on supply chains and competition.

content.content: Prices

Prices are rising at the fastest rate in four decades. Gas costs more. Groceries cost more. Supply chains are strained, and a war in Europe is about to make it worse. Whichever party is in power gets the blame.
Incumbents are protected. The left remembers.

insurgent_primaries.title: Primary Season
insurgent_primaries.subtitle: A bartender beats a ten-term congressman.

content.content: Primary Season

Insurgent left-wing candidates win a string of primaries, including a 28-year-old who unseats a senior House Democrat in New York. At the same time, moderates win a different set of swing-district primaries. The party's internal debate is now very public.
We prepare for disputed results and intimidation.
The Last Stretch

With three months until Election Day, the question is whether the coalition can turn discontent into turnout, and whether the party can persuade the persuadable. The stakes are as high as they have been in our lifetimes.
Rhetoric escalates. The temperature does not drop.

political_violence.title: Violence
political_violence.subtitle: A hostile year for democratic politics.

options.title: Fund security for officials and election workers.

content.content: Violence

Political violence reaches new heights: state lawmakers are shot, an activist is assassinated at a campus event, and threats against judges and election officials multiply. The temperature is far too high.
The party takes the biggest swing in its modern history. The base is on fire. The establishment is terrified. The general election is the test.

options.title: Let the voters decide, and mean it.

content.content: The Primary
The Iowa caucuses are weeks away. The front-runner has the endorsements, the money, and the delegates. The challenger has the crowds, the small donors, and an electrified left.
A rough, historic bet. The base is thrilled. The establishment is anxious.

options.title: Consolidate behind the former vice president.

content.content: The 2020 Primary
Two dozen candidates have entered. Only a few remain. The front-runners are a former vice president and a democratic-socialist senator. A South Carolina primary may decide it.
Their influence grows. So does the friction.
The Squad
A handful of insurgent freshmen clash openly with the Speaker. Social media amplifies everything. The press loves a civil war. Our opponents love it more.
Protests grow and stay peaceful, overwhelmingly.
Tariffs and Cuts

Broad tariffs rattle markets. Aid and research grants are frozen. Thousands of federal employees are dismissed. The administration claims a mandate. The courts, Congress, and the public all push back, unevenly.

trump_escalator.amplify.subtitle: A gamble that has side effects.

content.content: Some strategists decide he is the easiest opponent. The risk to the system is not their department.

trump_escalator.title: The Escalator
trump_escalator.subtitle: A television personality enters the race.

options.title: Take it seriously. Start building a contrast.
Quietly hope he wins the nomination.

content.content: The Escalator

A real-estate developer and television star descends a golden escalator to announce his candidacy for the Republican nomination, opening with a harsh attack on immigrants. Commentators call it a joke. The Republican field is crowded. His numbers are not a joke.
Attorneys general sue; courts block some actions and permit others.

options.title: Lawyer up and fight in court.

content.content: Inauguration

The new president takes the oath. Millions of people will march the next day. Within weeks, the administration issues a sweeping travel restriction, fires officials, and tests the boundaries of presidential power. The party's task is no longer to win a campaign but to defend the structure of the republic.
We decide that the voters will decide. Many wonder what norms are left.

options.title: Avoid impeachment. Focus on the election.

content.content: A Phone Call
A whistleblower alleges that the president pressed a foreign leader to investigate a political rival while withholding military aid. Pressure builds on the House to act. The Senate will not convict.
The politics are as hard as the law.
The checks reach people. So do the price tags.

opposition_strategy.cooperate.subtitle: Shows we can govern. Frustrates the base.

content.content: Governing means finding the votes that exist.

oversight.impeach.subtitle: Risky and polarizing, but sometimes necessary.

content.content: The Constitution gives the House this tool for a reason. Whether to use it is a judgment about the republic, about politics, and about what comes next.
Oversight and Investigations
With a congressional majority, we have subpoena power. Used well, it protects the republic. Used badly, it looks like a partisan show.

fundraise.pac.subtitle: +3 funds and a bit of media reach, at some cost in control.

content.content: Coordinated spending stretches every dollar, but the message gets harder to control.

fundraise.title: Fundraising
fundraise.subtitle: Money wins campaigns, and costs us something.

options.title: Coordinate with outside groups and PACs.

content.content: Fundraising
The party needs money for field offices, ads, and voter protection. The question is whose money.

messaging.identity.subtitle: Energizes the base; risks backlash with swing voters.

content.content: Representation matters. The question is whether we can say it in a way that persuades the people who are not already persuaded.

messaging.title: Message Discipline
messaging.subtitle: Decide what we are actually for.

options.title: Defense of democracy and the rule of law.

content.content: Message Discipline
A coalition of college graduates, workers, and minority voters cannot say everything at once. What do we lead with?
Lawyers, volunteers, and drives. Access to the ballot is a democratic good in itself, and a partisan one.
Grassroots Organizing
Votes do not collect themselves. Where should the field program go?

outreach.latino.subtitle: Shore up and grow a key bloc.

content.content: Organizers talk to voters in their languages, about their own priorities.
It works once.

party_unity.title: Party Unity Retreat
party_unity.subtitle: Bring the factions into one room.

options.title: Hold a long listening tour with every faction.

content.content: Party Unity Retreat
Everyone agrees we are on the same side. Everyone disagrees about the rest.
A better-informed public is a more stable one.
We make noise. Parts of the base love it. Moderates ask what the plan is.
The Return

The president takes the oath again, with unified control of Congress and a Supreme Court inclined to defer on executive power. In the first days come dozens of executive orders, mass pardons of January 6th defendants, a sweeping reshuffling of the civil service, and a campaign to shrink the federal government. The party is in the minority in both chambers.
We give their ideas a seat at the table. Some call it co-optation. Others call it politics.

sanders_enters.title: A Senator from Vermont
sanders_enters.subtitle: An insurgent challenge from the left.

options.title: Insist on a neutral, open primary.
Invite the insurgents into the platform process.

content.content: A Senator from Vermont

A democratic socialist senator from Vermont announces he will seek the Democratic nomination. Crowds are bigger than anyone expected. The establishment has a plan to coronate a front-runner. The question is how to treat the insurgency.
The effort fails when two senators refuse to go along. The voting-rights bills die.

reconciliation_standoff.title: Two Senators
reconciliation_standoff.subtitle: The filibuster and the reconciliation fight.

options.title: Pass the bipartisan infrastructure bill first.
Push for filibuster reform on voting rights.

content.content: Two Senators

Our majority in the Senate is 50 plus the Vice President. Two moderate Democratic senators block the more ambitious plans and refuse to change the filibuster. Activists threaten primaries. The Senate calendar slips.
Bruised But Standing

November 2026. American democracy has survived, but not unscathed. Trust is low, norms are frayed, and every institution has been tested. Whether the next generation inherits a working republic is still an open question.
Congress is in our hands, and the work of repair can begin.
Control of Congress is still contested, and so are the terms of repair.
Not a vote-winner. But it matters.

executive.title: Executive Action
executive.subtitle: What the President can do alone.

content.content: Executive Action
When Congress will not act, the executive branch can do a little. Courts and successors can undo it.

legislation.climate.subtitle: A long-run priority for the left and the young.

content.content: Tax credits, grants, and a durable investment framework.
Statehouses become laboratories, and bulwarks.

opposition_strategy.title: Opposition Strategy
opposition_strategy.subtitle: How do we resist from the minority?

options.title: Litigate. Use the courts and state attorneys general.
Support mass mobilization and peaceful protest.
Cooperate on the issues where we can.

content.content: Opposition Strategy
When the other side holds power, the opposition has to decide how to oppose.

outreach.independents.subtitle: Moderates and suburbanites respond to competence.

content.content: Tone, not just substance.
Coalition Outreach
The Democratic coalition has gaps. Where do we invest our time?

watchdog.security.subtitle: Reduces extremist threat. Risks civil-liberties backlash.

content.content: Threat assessments are quiet work. They are also controversial.

options.title: Support state-level secretaries of state and election officials.
Fund civic education and local news.
Quietly coordinate threat assessment with law enforcement.

content.content: Democracy Defense Program
When the rules are contested, they must be defended before the contest, not after.
A Hollowed Republic

November 2026. The republic still stands in name. The offices exist and the elections are held. But the protections that made them meaningful are thin, and the ones who would exploit that thinness are patient. The coming years will decide whether this is a low point or the new normal.
The reform is real and the backlash is also real.

legislation.border.subtitle: Politically costly with the base, and potentially with the right.

content.content: A deal like this is hard to get and harder to defend.

legislation.title: Legislative Push
legislation.subtitle: Move a bill, if we have the votes.

options.title: A bipartisan immigration and border package.

content.content: Legislative Push
Congress is where majorities are made real. What do we bring to the floor?
